title: حِكَايَةُ طَيْرِ الْمَاءِ وَالسِّحْلِفِ
part: Night 148 · The Hermit and the Pigeons ends / The Water-Bird and the Tortoise / The Wolf and the Fox begins
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 727–733 (Night 148, continuing directly from nights-147), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 148 ends the tale of the hermit and the pigeons: the pigeons multiply under his care and scatter when he dies. Then comes a pious shepherd who lives alone on a mountain among wild beasts. When he falls ill, God sends an angel in the form of a beautiful woman to test him; she offers herself, and he refuses her, covers his face with his cloak and turns to the remembrance of his Lord, and the angel goes back up to heaven. A holy man from a nearby village is told in a dream to seek the shepherd out. On the way he frightens the beasts and birds away from a spring, reproaches himself in verse, and on arriving stays to worship with the shepherd until death comes to them both. King Shahriyār says the tale has made him repent of killing women, and asks for tales of birds. A water-bird finds a corpse in a river, flees the vultures and eagles that gather on it, and is befriended by a tortoise, who consoles him on exile and grief; the two return to the island, and in a moment of contentment a hungry falcon kills the water-bird, because, it is said, he had neglected to praise God. Asked for tales of beasts, Shahrazād begins the tale of a fox and a wolf who share a den: the fox urges the overbearing wolf to gentleness, is struck senseless for it, and apologises in two lines of verse; the night breaks off there. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-eighth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْعَابِدَ قَدْ قَسَمَ قُوتَهُ نِصْفَيْنِ وَجَعَلَ نِصْفَهُ لِنَفْسِهِ وَنِصْفَهُ لِذَلِكَ الزَّوْجِ الْحَمَامِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿābida qad qasama qūtahu niṣfayni wa-jaʿala niṣfahu li-nafsihi wa-niṣfahu li-dhālika al-zawji al-ḥamāmi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the worshipper had divided his sustenance (into) two halves, and made half-of-it for himself and half-of-it for that pair, the pigeons.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the hermit divided his food into two halves, keeping one half for himself and giving the other to that pair of pigeons.
sentences.n: The sentence the last night broke off is taken up again. al-zawji al-ḥamāmi, literally “the pair, the pigeons”: the print sets the two nouns side by side with the article on both, where Classical Arabic would say zawj al-ḥamām, “the pair of pigeons”. It recurs below.

sentences.t: وَدَعَا الْعَابِدُ لَهُمَا بِكَثْرَةِ النَّسْلِ فَكَثُرَ نَسْلُهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-daʿā al-ʿābidu lahumā bi-kathrati al-nasli fa-kathura nasluhumā
sentences.l: And the worshipper prayed for-them for abundance of the offspring, so their offspring became-abundant.
sentences.i: The hermit prayed that they might have many young, and their young grew many.
sentences.n: daʿā li-, “to pray for (someone)”; bi- names what is prayed for: “prayed for them, for abundance of offspring”. nasl, “offspring, progeny”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَكُنِ الْحَمَامُ يَأْوِي سِوَى الْجَبَلِ الَّذِي فِيهِ الْعَابِدُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yakuni al-ḥamāmu yaʾwī siwā al-jabali alladhī fīhi al-ʿābidu
sentences.l: And the pigeons were not taking-shelter (in anything) except the mountain which in-it (was) the worshipper.
sentences.i: The pigeons made their home on no mountain but the one where the hermit lived.
sentences.n: awā, yaʾwī, “to take shelter, to lodge”, usually with ilā; here it takes its object directly. siwā, “other than, except”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ السَّبَبُ فِي اجْتِمَاعِ الْحَمَامِ بِالْعَابِدِ كَثْرَةَ تَسْبِيحِ الْحَمَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-sababu fī ijtimāʿi al-ḥamāmi bi-al-ʿābidi kathrata tasbīḥi al-ḥamāmi
sentences.l: And the cause in the gathering of the pigeons with the worshipper was the abundance of the glorifying of the pigeons.
sentences.i: The reason the pigeons kept company with the hermit was that they so often sang the praises of God.
sentences.n: ijtimāʿ bi-, “meeting with, keeping company with”. tasbīḥ, saying subḥāna allāh, “glory be to God”: praising God. The cooing of doves was commonly heard as such praise.

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ إِنَّ الْحَمَامَ يَقُولُ فِي تَسْبِيحِهِ سُبْحَانَ خَالِقِ الْخَلْقِ وَقَاسِمِ الرِّزْقِ وَبَانِى السَّمٰوَاتِ وَبَاسِطِ الْأَرَضِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla inna al-ḥamāma yaqūlu fī tasbīḥihi subḥāna khāliqi al-khalqi wa-qāsimi al-rizqi wa-bānī al-samāwāti wa-bāsiṭi al-araḍīna
sentences.l: And it-was-said that the pigeon says in its glorifying: Glory (to) the Creator of the creation, and the Divider of the provision, and the Builder of the heavens, and the Spreader-out of the earths.
sentences.i: It is said that in its praises the pigeon says: “Glory to the Creator of all creatures, who apportions their daily bread, who built the heavens and spread out the earths.”
sentences.n: qīla, “it was said”, the passive of qāla, used to pass on a report. The praise is a string of four titles of God, each an active participle with its object: khāliq al-khalq, qāsim al-rizq (rizq, “provision, livelihood”), bānī al-samāwāt, bāsiṭ al-araḍīn. The first two rhyme, khalq/rizq loosely. بانى is the print's spelling with ى; al-araḍūn, “the earths”, the rare plural of arḍ, as in the sevenfold earths answering the seven heavens.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ ذَلِكَ الزَّوْجُ الْحَمَامُ فِي أَرْغَدِ عَيْشٍ هُوَ وَنَسْلُهُ حَتَّى مَاتَ الْعَابِدُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal dhālika al-zawju al-ḥamāmu fī arghadi ʿayshin huwa wa-nasluhu ḥattā māta al-ʿābidu
sentences.l: And that pair, the pigeons, did not cease (to be) in the most-plentiful of living, it and its offspring, until the worshipper died.
sentences.i: That pair of pigeons and their young lived in the greatest plenty until the hermit died.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “did not cease”, “went on (being)”. arghad, elative of raghīd, “ample, easy (of life)”: “the most ample of living”.

sentences.t: فَتَشَتَّتَ شَمْلُ الْحَمَامِ وَتَفَرَّقَ فِى الْمُدُنِ وَالْقُرَى وَالْجِبَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-tashattata shamlu al-ḥamāmi wa-tafarraqa fī al-muduni wa-al-qurā wa-al-jibāli
sentences.l: Then the gathered-company of the pigeons was-scattered, and it dispersed in the cities and the villages and the mountains.
sentences.i: Then the pigeons' company broke up and scattered among the cities, the villages and the mountains.
sentences.n: tashattata shamluhum, “their union was scattered”, a set phrase for a family or company breaking apart; shaml is what holds a group together. The shaddas on فتشتّت and وتفرّق are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ إِنَّهُ كَانَ فِي بَعْضِ الْجِبَالِ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الرُّعَاةِ وَكَانَ صَاحِبَ دِينٍ وَعَقْلٍ وَعِفَّةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla innahu kāna fī baʿḍi al-jibāli rajulun mina al-ruʿāti wa-kāna ṣāḥiba dīnin wa-ʿaqlin wa-ʿiffatin
sentences.l: And it-was-said that there was in one of the mountains a man of the shepherds, and he was a possessor of religion and reason and chastity.
sentences.i: It is also told that on a certain mountain there was a shepherd, a man of piety, good sense and chastity.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, of the pious shepherd. ruʿāt, plural of rāʿī, “shepherd, herdsman”. ṣāḥib, “companion, owner”, before an abstract noun: “a man of”. ʿiffa, “chastity, continence”, which the tale is about to test.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لَهُ أَغْنَامًا يَرْعَاهَا وَيَنْتَفِعُ بِأَلْبَانِهَا وَأَصْوَافِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lahu aghnāman yarʿāhā wa-yantafiʿu bi-albānihā wa-aṣwāfihā
sentences.l: And there were for him sheep he pastured-them and he benefited by their milks and their wools.
sentences.i: He had flocks of sheep which he pastured, living on their milk and their wool.
sentences.n: kāna lahu aghnāman: Classical Arabic would make the subject nominative, aghnāmun, “he had sheep”; the print has the accusative, as if after kāna, a common Middle Arabic habit. aghnām, plural of ghanam, “sheep (and goats), a flock”. intafaʿa bi-, “to make use of, benefit from”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْجَبَلُ الَّذِى يَأْوِي إِلَيْهِ الرَّاعِي كَثِيرَ الْأَشْجَارِ وَالْمَرْعَى وَالسِّبَاعِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-jabalu alladhī yaʾwī ilayhi al-rāʿī kathīra al-ashjāri wa-al-marʿā wa-al-sibāʿi
sentences.l: And that mountain which the shepherd took-shelter to-it was abundant of the trees and the pasture and the beasts-of-prey.
sentences.i: The mountain where the shepherd lived was rich in trees and pasture, and full of wild beasts.
sentences.n: kathīr al-, “abundant in”, an adjective governing a noun: “many-treed”. sibāʿ, plural of sabuʿ, “beast of prey” (lion, wolf and the like). The hamza in يأوي is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لِتِلْكَ الْوُحُوشِ قُدْرَةٌ عَلَى الرَّاعِي وَلَا عَلَى غَنَمِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yakun li-tilka al-wuḥūshi qudratun ʿalā al-rāʿī wa-lā ʿalā ghanamihi
sentences.l: And there was not for those wild-beasts power over the shepherd nor over his sheep.
sentences.i: Yet those wild beasts had no power over the shepherd or his flock.
sentences.n: qudra ʿalā, “power over”. wuḥūsh, plural of waḥsh, “wild animal”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مُقِيمًا فِى الْجَبَلِ مُطْمَئِنًّا لَا يَهُمُّهُ شَيْءٌ مِنْ أَمْرِ الدُّنْيَا لِسَعَادَتِهِ وَإِقْبَالِهِ عَلَى صَلَوٰتِهِ وَعِبَادَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal muqīman fī al-jabali muṭmaʾinnan lā yahummuhu shayʾun min amri al-dunyā li-saʿādatihi wa-iqbālihi ʿalā ṣalawātihi wa-ʿibādatihi
sentences.l: And he did not cease (being) dwelling in the mountain, at-peace, nothing of the affair of the world concerning-him, because-of his happiness and his turning-toward his prayers and his worship.
sentences.i: He lived on in the mountain at peace, untroubled by any of the world's affairs, so happy was he and so devoted to his prayers and worship.
sentences.n: muṭmaʾinn, “tranquil, at rest”. hammahu, “to concern, worry”. al-dunyā, “the nearer (life)”, this world, as against the hereafter. iqbāl ʿalā, “turning one's face toward, applying oneself to”. صلوٰته is the print's spelling with the dagger alif, as in the Qurʾān; read here as the plural ṣalawātihi, “his prayers” (the singular ṣalātihi is also possible).

sentences.t: فَقَدَّرَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ مَرِضَ مَرَضًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qaddara allāhu annahu mariḍa maraḍan shadīdan
sentences.l: Then God decreed that he fell-sick a severe sickness.
sentences.i: Then God ordained that he should fall gravely ill.
sentences.n: qaddara, “to decree, ordain”: the turn of fate that begins the trial. maraḍan shadīdan, the verb's own noun as an emphatic object: “sickened a severe sickening”.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ الْعَابِدُ فِي كَهْفِ الْجَبَلِ وَصَارَتِ الْغَنَمُ تَخْرُجُ بِالنَّهَارِ إِلَى مَرْعَاهَا وَتَأْوِي بِاللَّيْلِ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala al-ʿābidu fī kahfi al-jabali wa-ṣārati al-ghanamu takhruju bi-al-nahāri ilā marʿāhā wa-taʾwī bi-al-layli ilā al-kahfi
sentences.l: So the worshipper entered into the cave of the mountain, and the sheep began going-out by the day to their pasture and taking-shelter by the night to the cave.
sentences.i: The hermit took to a cave in the mountain, and his sheep would go out by day to their pasture and come back at night to the cave.
sentences.n: The shepherd is now called al-ʿābid, “the worshipper, the hermit”, as the tale goes on to do. ṣāra with an imperfect verb, “began to, took to (doing)”. bi-al-nahāri … bi-al-layli, “by day … by night”. The hamza in وتأوي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَرَادَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى أَنْ يَخْتَبِرَ ذَلِكَ الرَّاعِيَ وَيَمْتَحِنَهُ فِي طَاعَتِهِ وَصَبْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-arāda allāhu taʿālā an yakhtabira dhālika al-rāʿiya wa-yamtaḥinahu fī ṭāʿatihi wa-ṣabrihi
sentences.l: Then God, (may He be) exalted, willed to test that shepherd and to try-him in his obedience and his patience.
sentences.i: Then God Most High willed to test that shepherd and to try his obedience and his patience.
sentences.n: taʿālā, “may He be exalted”, the customary blessing after the name of God. ikhtabara and imtaḥana both mean “to test, to put to the proof”: a doubled pair for weight.

sentences.t: فَبَعَثَ إِلَيْهِ مَلَكًا فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ الْمَلَكُ فِي صُورَةِ امْرَأَةٍ حَسْنَاءَ فَجَلَسَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿatha ilayhi malakan fa-dakhala ʿalayhi al-malaku fī ṣūrati imraʾatin ḥasnāʾa fa-jalasa bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: So He sent to-him an angel, and the angel entered upon-him in the form of a beautiful woman, and he sat between his two-hands.
sentences.i: So He sent an angel to him, and the angel came in to him in the form of a beautiful woman and sat down before him.
sentences.n: malak, “angel”, not malik, “king”: the two are spelt alike, ملك. The angel stays grammatically masculine, fa-jalasa, “he sat”, even in a woman's form; once the shepherd sees it, it is “that woman” and “she”. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, i.e. “in front of him”. ḥasnāʾ, “beautiful (woman)”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الرَّاعِي تِلْكَ الْمَرْأَةَ جَالِسَةً عِنْدَهُ اقْشَعَرَّ بَدَنُهُ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-rāʿī tilka al-marʾata jālisatan ʿindahu iqshaʿarra badanuhu minhā
sentences.l: And when the shepherd saw that woman sitting by-him, his body shuddered from-her.
sentences.i: When the shepherd saw the woman sitting beside him, his flesh crept at the sight of her.
sentences.n: The print has انشعرّ, a misprint for اقشعرّ, corrected here. iqshaʿarra, “to shudder, to bristle”: the skin creeping with fear or revulsion. The shadda on its rāʾ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَيَّتُهَا الْمَرْأَةُ مَا الَّذِي دَعَاكِ إِلَى الْمَجِيءِ هُنَا وَلَيْسَ لِي حَاجَةٌ بِكِ وَلَابَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكِ مَا يُوجِبُ لِدُخُولِكِ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ayyatuhā al-marʾatu mā alladhī daʿāki ilā al-majīʾi hunā wa-laysa lī ḥājatun biki wa-lā baynī wa-baynaki mā yūjibu li-dukhūliki ʿindī
sentences.l: And he said to-her: O you the woman, what (is) the-thing-which called-you to the coming here, and there-is-not for-me need of-you, nor between-me and between-you (is there) what requires for your entering with-me?
sentences.i: He said to her, “Woman, what brought you here? I have no need of you, and there is nothing between us that calls for your coming in to me.”
sentences.n: ayyatuhā, the feminine of ayyuhā, “O you”; the shadda on ايّتها is the print's. ḥāja bi-, “need of”. The print runs wa-lā baynī together as ولابيني; the spacing is kept. awjaba, “to make necessary”, normally takes a direct object; li- before dukhūliki is a looser, colloquial construction.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْإِنْسَانُ أَمَا تَرَي حُسْنِي وَجَمَالِي وَطِيبَ رَائِحَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ayyuhā al-insānu a-mā tarā ḥusnī wa-jamālī wa-ṭība rāʾiḥatī
sentences.l: And she said to-him: O you the human, do-you not see my beauty and my comeliness and the sweetness of my scent?
sentences.i: She said, “Man, do you not see my beauty, my loveliness and the sweetness of my scent?
sentences.n: a-mā, “is it not that…?”, a question expecting yes. تري is the print's spelling of tarā, “you see”, with ي for final ى. rāʾiḥa, “smell, scent”.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَعْلَمُ حَاجَةَ النِّسَاءِ مِنَ الرِّجَالِ وَالرِّجَالِ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ فَمَا الَّذِي يَمْنَعُكَ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: a-mā taʿlamu ḥājata al-nisāʾi mina al-rijāli wa-al-rijāli mina al-nisāʾi fa-mā alladhī yamnaʿuka minnī
sentences.l: Do-you not know the need of the women from the men, and of the men from the women? So what (is) the-thing-which holds-you-back from-me?
sentences.i: Do you not know what women need of men, and men of women? What, then, keeps you from me?
sentences.n: wa-al-rijāli, genitive, still governed by ḥājata: “(the need) of men”. The shadda on منّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اخْتَرْتُ قُرْبَكَ وَأَحْبَبْتُ وِصَالَكَ وَقَدْ جِئْتُكَ طَائِعَةً وَعَلَيْكَ غَيْرَ مُمْتَنِعَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi ikhtartu qurbaka wa-aḥbabtu wiṣālaka wa-qad jiʾtuka ṭāʾiʿatan wa-ʿalayka ghayra mumtaniʿatin
sentences.l: And I have chosen nearness-to-you and loved union-with-you, and I have come-to-you willing, and toward-you not refusing.
sentences.i: I have chosen to be near you and longed to be joined with you; I have come to you of my own will, and I will not hold back from you.
sentences.n: wiṣāl, “union”, the lovers' word for coming together. ṭāʾiʿatan … ghayra mumtaniʿatin, two circumstantial accusatives, “obedient … unrefusing”, rhyming in -iʿatan: her speech falls into sajʿ. ʿalayka ghayra mumtaniʿatin, “not refusing myself to you”.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ عِنْدَنَا أَحَدٌ نَخْشَاهُ وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أُقِيمَ مَعَكَ طُولَ مُقَامِكَ فِي هَذَا الْجَبَلِ وَأَكُونَ أَنِيسَةً لَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa ʿindanā aḥadun nakhshāhu wa-urīdu an uqīma maʿaka ṭūla muqāmika fī hādhā al-jabali wa-akūna anīsatan laka
sentences.l: And there-is-not with-us anyone we-fear-him, and I-want that I-stay with-you (the) length of your staying in this mountain, and I-be a companion for-you.
sentences.i: There is no one here for us to fear. I want to stay with you as long as you live on this mountain, and be your companion.
sentences.n: aḥadun nakhshāhu, a relative clause without a relative pronoun, normal after an indefinite noun: “anyone (whom) we fear”. ṭūla, “for the length of”, an adverbial accusative. anīsa, “companion, one who keeps (you) company and cheers (you)”.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ عَرَضْتُ نَفْسِي عَلَيْكَ لِأَنَّكَ تَحْتَاجُ لِخِدْمَةِ النِّسَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-qad ʿaraḍtu nafsī ʿalayka li-annaka taḥtāju li-khidmati al-nisāʾi
sentences.l: For I have offered myself to-you, because you need the service of the women.
sentences.i: I offer myself to you, for you are in need of a woman's care.
sentences.n: ʿaraḍa nafsahu ʿalā, “to offer oneself to”. iḥtāja, “to need”, Classical with ilā; li- is the looser usage.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ إِنْ بَاشَرْتَنِي زَالَ عَنْكَ مَرَضُكَ وَعَادَتْ إِلَيْكَ صِحَّتُكَ وَنَدِمْتَ عَلَى مَا فَاتَكَ مِنْ قُرْبِ النِّسَاءِ فِي سَالِفِ عُمْرِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta in bāshartanī zāla ʿanka maraḍuka wa-ʿādat ilayka ṣiḥḥatuka wa-nadimta ʿalā mā fātaka min qurbi al-nisāʾi fī sālifi ʿumrika
sentences.l: And you, if you have-lain-with-me, your sickness will-leave from-you, and your health will-return to-you, and you will-regret what passed-you-by of the nearness of the women in the bygone of your life.
sentences.i: If you lie with me, your sickness will leave you and your health come back, and you will regret all the closeness to women you missed in the years gone by.
sentences.n: bāshara, “to touch skin to skin”, hence “to lie with, have intercourse with”. After in, “if”, the past tenses read as future: zāla, ʿādat, nadimta, “will leave, will return, you will regret”. fātahu, “it escaped him, he missed it”. sālif ʿumrika, “the past of your life”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ نَصَحْتُكَ فَاقْبَلْ نُصْحِي وَادْنُ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: wa-qad naṣaḥtuka fa-iqbal nuṣḥī wa-udnu minnī
sentences.l: And I have counselled-you, so accept my counsel and draw-near to-me.
sentences.i: I have given you good counsel: take it, and come close to me.”
sentences.n: udnu, imperative of danā, yadnū, “to come near”. The shadda on منّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الرَّاعِي اخْرُجِي عَنِّي أَيَّتُهَا الْمَرْأَةُ الْخَدَّاعَةُ الْغَدَّارَةُ فَلَا أَرْكَنُ إِلَيْكِ وَلَا أَدْنُو مِنْكِ وَلَا حَاجَةَ لِي بِقُرْبِكِ وَلَا بِوِصَالِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-rāʿī ukhrujī ʿannī ayyatuhā al-marʾatu al-khaddāʿatu al-ghaddāratu fa-lā arkanu ilayki wa-lā adnū minki wa-lā ḥājata lī bi-qurbiki wa-lā bi-wiṣāliki
sentences.l: And the shepherd said to-her: Go-out from-me, O you the woman, the deceiving-one, the betraying-one, for I-do-not lean on-you, nor draw-near to-you, and (there is) no need for-me of nearness-to-you nor of union-with-you.
sentences.i: The shepherd said to her, “Get away from me, you deceitful, treacherous woman! I will not rely on you or come near you; I have no need of your closeness or your embraces.
sentences.n: khaddāʿa, ghaddāra, intensive forms, “full of deceit, full of treachery”, rhyming. rakana ilā, “to lean on, put one's trust in”.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّ مَنْ رَغِبَ فِيكِ زَهِدَ فِى الْآخِرَةِ وَمَنْ رَغِبَ فِى الْآخِرَةِ زَهِدَ فِيكِ لِأَنَّكِ فَتَنْتِ الْأَوَّلِينَ وَالْآخِرِينَ وَاللَّهُ تَعَالَى لِعِبَادِهِ بِالْمِرْصَادِ
sentences.tr: li-anna man raghiba fīki zahida fī al-ākhirati wa-man raghiba fī al-ākhirati zahida fīki li-annaki fatanti al-awwalīna wa-al-ākhirīna wa-allāhu taʿālā li-ʿibādihi bi-al-mirṣādi
sentences.l: Because whoever desires in-you renounces in the hereafter, and whoever desires in the hereafter renounces in-you, because you have-tempted the first-ones and the last-ones, and God, (may He be) exalted, (is) for His servants at the watch-post.
sentences.i: For whoever desires you turns his back on the hereafter, and whoever desires the hereafter turns his back on you. You have led astray the first generations and the last, and God Most High lies in wait for His servants.
sentences.n: raghiba fī, “to desire”; zahida fī, “to renounce, to want nothing of”: the two verbs trade places in a chiasmus. The shepherd speaks to the woman as preachers speak of the world, al-dunyā, the seductress in the sermons. al-awwalīn wa-al-ākhirīn, “the former and the later”, all mankind. bi-al-mirṣād, “at the watch-post”, echoing Qurʾān 89:14, inna rabbaka la-bi-al-mirṣād: God watches and will call to account. The hamza in الآخرة and والآخرين is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَالْوَيْلُ لِمَنِ ابْتُلِىَ بِصُحْبَتِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-waylu li-mani ubtuliya bi-ṣuḥbatiki
sentences.l: And the woe (is) for whoever was-afflicted with your company.
sentences.i: Woe to the man who is afflicted with your company!”
sentences.n: al-wayl li-, “woe to”. ubtuliya, passive of ibtalā, “to try, afflict”, spelt by the print with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَيُّهَا التَّايِهُ عَنِ السَّدَادِ وَالضَّالُّ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الرَّشَادِ أَقْبِلْ بِوَجْهِكَ إِلَيَّ وَانْظُرْ إِلَى مَحَاسِنِي وَاغْتَنِمْ قُرْبِي كَمَا فَعَلَ مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَكَ مِنَ الْحُكَمَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ayyuhā al-tāyihu ʿani al-sadādi wa-al-ḍāllu ʿan ṭarīqi al-rashādi aqbil bi-wajhika ilayya wa-unẓur ilā maḥāsinī wa-ightanim qurbī kamā faʿala man kāna qablaka mina al-ḥukamāʾi
sentences.l: And she said to-him: O you the stray from the right-aim, and the wanderer from the path of the right-guidance, turn with your face to-me, and look at my charms, and seize-the-gain-of nearness-to-me, as did who was before-you of the wise-men.
sentences.i: She said to him, “You who have strayed from what is right and wandered from the path of good guidance, turn your face to me, look upon my charms, and make the most of my nearness, as the sages before you did.
sentences.n: التايه is the print's spelling of al-tāʾih, “the one who has lost his way”, with ي for the hamza. sadād and rashād rhyme: she answers his sermon in sajʿ. aqbala bi-wajhihi ilā, “to turn one's face toward”. ightanama, “to take as booty, seize the chance of”. The shaddas on والضالّ and اليّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِنْكَ تَجْرِبَةً وَأَصْوَبَ مِنْكَ رَأْيًا وَمَعَ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَرْفُضُوا مَا رَفَضْتَ مِنَ التَّمَتُّعِ بِالنِّسَاءِ بَلْ رَغِبُوا فِيمَا زَهِدْتَ فِيهِ مِنْ مُبَاشَرَةِ النِّسَاءِ وَقُرْبِهِنَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qad kānū akthara minka tajribatan wa-aṣwaba minka raʾyan wa-maʿa dhālika lam yarfuḍū mā rafaḍta mina al-tamattuʿi bi-al-nisāʾi bal raghibū fīmā zahidta fīhi min mubāsharati al-nisāʾi wa-qurbihinna
sentences.l: For they were more than-you in experience and more-right than-you in judgement, and with that they did-not reject what you-rejected of the enjoyment of the women; rather they desired what you-renounced of the lying-with the women and nearness-to-them.
sentences.i: They had more experience than you and sounder judgement, and yet they did not refuse what you refuse, the enjoyment of women; on the contrary, they desired what you renounce, lying with women and being close to them.
sentences.n: akthara … tajribatan, aṣwaba … raʾyan: elatives with an accusative of specification, “more in experience, more right in judgement”. tamattuʿ bi-, “taking pleasure in”. She turns his own word zahida back on him.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَسَاءَهُمْ ذَلِكَ فِي دِينِهِمْ وَلَا دُنْيَاهُمْ فَارْجِعْ عَنْ رَأْيِكَ تَحْمَدْ عَاقِبَةَ أَمْرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā asāʾahum dhālika fī dīnihim wa-lā dunyāhum fa-irjiʿ ʿan raʾyika taḥmad ʿāqibata amrika
sentences.l: So that did-not harm-them in their religion nor their world; so turn-back from your opinion, (and) you-will-praise the outcome of your affair.
sentences.i: It did them no harm in their faith or in their worldly life. So give up your opinion, and you will be glad of how things turn out for you.”
sentences.n: asāʾa, “to do harm to, to trouble”, here with a direct object. dīn wa-dunyā, “religion and world”, a fixed pair for the whole of a life. taḥmad, jussive in answer to the imperative irjiʿ: “turn back, (and) you will praise”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الرَّاعِي إِنَّ كُلَّمَا تَقُولِينَهُ نَكِرْتُهُ وَكَرِهْتُهُ وَجَمِيعَ مَا تُبْدِينَهُ زَهِدْتُهُ لِأَنَّكِ خَدَّاعَةٌ غَدَّارَةٌ لَا عَهْدَ لَكِ وَلَا وَفَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-rāʿī inna kullamā taqūlīnahu nakirtuhu wa-karihtuhu wa-jamīʿa mā tubdīnahu zahidtuhu li-annaki khaddāʿatun ghaddāratun lā ʿahda laki wa-lā wafāʾa
sentences.l: And the shepherd said to-her: Indeed everything-that you-say-it, I-have-disowned-it and I-have-hated-it, and all that you-show-it I-have-renounced-it, because you (are) deceiving, betraying; no covenant (is) for-you and no faithfulness.
sentences.i: The shepherd said to her, “Everything you say I reject and loathe, and all that you display I spurn, for you are deceitful and treacherous; you keep no pact and no faith.
sentences.n: كلما is written as one word, as the print often does for kull mā, “all that”; here it is not the conjunction kullamā, “whenever”, but “everything that”. nakira, “to disown, not acknowledge”. abdā, “to show, display”. ʿahd and wafāʾ, “pledge” and “keeping faith”. The shadda on غدّارة is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَكَمْ مِنْ قَبِيحٍ تَحْتَ حُسْنِكِ أَخْفَيْتِهِ وَكَمْ مِنْ صَالِحٍ فَتَنْتِهِ وَكَانَتْ عَاقِبَتُهُ إِلَى النَّدَامَةِ وَالْخُسْرَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-kam min qabīḥin taḥta ḥusniki akhfaytihi wa-kam min ṣāliḥin fatantihi wa-kānat ʿāqibatuhu ilā al-nadāmati wa-al-khusrāni
sentences.l: For how-much of ugly (thing) under your beauty you-have-hidden-it, and how-many of righteous (man) you-have-tempted-him, and his outcome was to the regret and the loss!
sentences.i: How much ugliness you have hidden beneath your beauty, and how many good men you have led astray, whose end was remorse and ruin!
sentences.n: kam min, “how many a …!”, exclamatory, with the noun in the genitive after min. fatana, “to tempt, lead into trial”. nadāma and khusrān, “regret” and “loss”, a pair that closes many a moral tale.

sentences.t: فَارْجِعِي عَنِّي أَيَّتُهَا الْمُصْلِحَةُ نَفْسَهَا لِفَسَادِ غَيْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-irjiʿī ʿannī ayyatuhā al-muṣliḥatu nafsahā li-fasādi ghayrihā
sentences.l: So go-back from-me, O you the one-who-makes-good herself for the corruption of others-than-her.
sentences.i: Go away from me, you who adorn yourself to bring others to ruin!”
sentences.n: al-muṣliḥa nafsahā, “she who puts herself in good order”, i.e. makes herself fair and fine; the active participle takes nafsahā as its object. iṣlāḥ and fasād, “setting right” and “corrupting”, are set against each other.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَلْقَى عَبَاءَتَهُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ حَتَّى لَا يَرَى وَجْهَهَا وَاشْتَغَلَ بِذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ
sentences.tr: thumma alqā ʿabāʾatahu ʿalā wajhihi ḥattā lā yarā wajhahā wa-ishtaghala bi-dhikri rabbihi
sentences.l: Then he threw his cloak over his face so-that he would-not see her face, and he occupied-himself with the remembrance of his Lord.
sentences.i: Then he threw his cloak over his face so as not to see hers, and gave himself up to the remembrance of his Lord.
sentences.n: ʿabāʾa, a wide, sleeveless woollen cloak. dhikr, “remembrance”: calling on God's names in prayer. ishtaghala bi-, “to busy oneself with”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمَلَكُ حُسْنَ طَاعَتِهِ خَرَجَ عَنْهُ وَصَعِدَ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-malaku ḥusna ṭāʿatihi kharaja ʿanhu wa-ṣaʿida ilā al-samāʾi
sentences.l: And when the angel saw the goodness of his obedience, he went-out from-him and ascended to the sky.
sentences.i: When the angel saw how well he obeyed, it left him and rose up to heaven.
sentences.n: The angel is again al-malak, masculine, now that the test is over. samāʾ, “sky, heaven”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ قَرِيبًا مِنَ الرَّاعِي قَرْيَةٌ فِيهَا رَجُلٌ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِمَكَانِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna qarīban mina al-rāʿī qaryatun fīhā rajulun mina al-ṣāliḥīna lam yaʿlam bi-makānihi
sentences.l: And there was near to the shepherd a village, in-it a man of the righteous-ones, (who) did-not know of his place.
sentences.i: Not far from the shepherd there was a village, and in it lived a righteous man who did not know where the shepherd was.
sentences.n: kāna qarīban … qaryatun: the predicate, qarīban, comes first and the subject, qaryatun, last; kāna stays masculine before it. ʿalima bi-, “to know of”. The ṣāliḥ, “righteous man”, is the second worshipper of the tale.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى فِي مَنَامِهِ كَأَنَّ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ لَهُ إِنَّ بِالْقُرْبِ مِنْكَ فِي مَكَانِ كَذَا رَجُلٌ صَالِحٌ فَاذْهَبْ إِلَيْهِ وَكُنْ تَحْتَ طَاعَةِ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾā fī manāmihi ka-anna qāʾilan yaqūlu lahu inna bi-al-qurbi minka fī makāni kadhā rajulun ṣāliḥun fa-idhhab ilayhi wa-kun taḥta ṭāʿati amrihi
sentences.l: And he saw in his sleep as-if a sayer was saying to-him: Indeed near to-you, in a place (of) such-and-such, (is) a righteous man, so go to-him and be under the obedience of his command.
sentences.i: He saw in a dream someone who seemed to say to him, “Near you, in such-and-such a place, there is a righteous man. Go to him and put yourself under his command.”
sentences.n: manām, “sleep, dream”. ka-anna, “as if”: dreams are reported this way in Arabic. inna … rajulun: after inna the subject should be accusative, rajulan, but the print leaves it nominative, a common Middle Arabic habit. fī makāni kadhā, “in such-and-such a place”: the teller does not name it. The hamza in كأن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ تَوَجَّهَ نَحْوَهُ سَائِرًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu tawajjaha naḥwahu sāʾiran
sentences.l: And when the morning became-morning, he turned-his-face toward-him, travelling.
sentences.i: In the morning he set out on foot toward him.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, a stock phrase. tawajjaha naḥwa, “to head toward”. sāʾiran, “journeying”, a circumstantial accusative. The shadda on توجّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اشْتَدَّ عَلَيْهِ الْحَرُّ انْتَهَى إِلَى شَجَرَةٍ عِنْدَهَا عَيْنُ مَاءٍ تَجْرِي فَاسْتَرَاحَ هُنَاكَ وَجَلَسَ فِي ظِلِّ تِلْكَ الشَّجَرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ishtadda ʿalayhi al-ḥarru intahā ilā shajaratin ʿindahā ʿaynu māʾin tajrī fa-istarāḥa hunāka wa-jalasa fī ẓilli tilka al-shajarati
sentences.l: And when the heat grew-hard upon-him, he came to a tree by-it a spring of water flowing, so he rested there and sat in the shade of that tree.
sentences.i: When the heat bore hard on him, he came to a tree beside a running spring, and there he rested, sitting in the tree's shade.
sentences.n: intahā ilā, “to reach, arrive at”. ʿayn māʾ, “an eye of water”, a spring. The shaddas on اشتدّ and الحرّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا هُوَ بِوُحُوشٍ وَطُيُورٍ أَتَوْا إِلَى تِلْكَ الْعَيْنِ لِيَشْرَبُوا مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-idhā huwa bi-wuḥūshin wa-ṭuyūrin ataw ilā tilka al-ʿayni li-yashrabū minhā
sentences.l: And behold, he (was) with wild-beasts and birds (that) came to that spring to drink from-it.
sentences.i: And then wild beasts and birds came to the spring to drink.
sentences.n: fa-idhā huwa bi-, “and behold, he (was faced) with”: idhā of surprise, with bi- marking what suddenly appears. ataw and li-yashrabū are masculine plural, the form for persons, used here of animals, as colloquial Arabic does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوُا الْعَابِدَ جَالِسًا نَفَرُوا مِنْهُ وَرَجَعُوا وَشَرَدُوا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawu al-ʿābida jālisan nafarū minhu wa-rajaʿū wa-sharadū
sentences.l: And when they saw the worshipper sitting, they shied from-him and went-back and fled.
sentences.i: But when they saw the hermit sitting there, they shied away from him, turned back and fled.
sentences.n: nafara min, “to shy away from, take fright at”. sharada, “to run off, stray”, of animals. The hamza in رأوا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعَابِدُ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ إِنِّي لَمْ أَسْتَرِحْ هُنَا إِلَّا ضَرَرًا عَلَى هَذِهِ الْوُحُوشِ وَالطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿābidu lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāhi innī lam astariḥ hunā illā ḍararan ʿalā hādhihi al-wuḥūshi wa-al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: And the worshipper said: There-is-no strength and no power except by God! Indeed-I have-not rested here except (as) a harm upon these wild-beasts and the birds.
sentences.i: The hermit said, “There is no strength and no power save in God! My resting here has brought nothing but harm to these beasts and birds.”
sentences.n: lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāh, said at a mishap or a fault in oneself. The print runs lā ḥawla together as لاحول; the spacing is kept. lam astariḥ … illā ḍararan, “I have not rested except (as) harm”: a loose, compressed turn, meaning his rest has been nothing but a harm to them. The shadda on الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ وَقَالَ مُعَاتِبًا لِنَفْسِهِ لَقَدْ أَضَرَّ بِهَذِهِ الْحَيَوَانَاتِ فِي هَذَا الْيَوْمِ جُلُوسِي فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma wa-qāla muʿātiban li-nafsihi la-qad aḍarra bi-hādhihi al-ḥayawānāti fī hādhā al-yawmi julūsī fī hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: So he rose and said, reproaching (to) himself: Truly has harmed these animals on this day my sitting in this place.
sentences.i: So he got up and said, reproaching himself, “Truly, my sitting in this place has done these creatures harm today.
sentences.n: muʿātiban li-nafsihi, “upbraiding himself”. aḍarra bi-, “to harm”. The subject, julūsī, “my sitting”, comes at the end, after the verb and its object. The shadda on اضرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَمَا الْعُذْرُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ خَالِقِي وَخَالِقِ هَذِهِ الطُّيُورِ وَالْوُحُوشِ فَإِنِّي كُنْتُ سَبَبًا لِشُرُودِهِمْ عَنْ شُرْبِهِمْ وَعَنْ رِزْقِهِمْ وَمَرْعَاهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-mā al-ʿudhru baynī wa-bayna khāliqī wa-khāliqi hādhihi al-ṭuyūri wa-al-wuḥūshi fa-innī kuntu sababan li-shurūdihim ʿan shurbihim wa-ʿan rizqihim wa-marʿāhum
sentences.l: So what (is) the excuse between-me and between my Creator and the Creator of these birds and the wild-beasts? For indeed-I was a cause for their running-off from their drinking and from their provision and their pasture.
sentences.i: What excuse can I offer my Creator, who created these birds and beasts too? For I have been the cause of their fleeing from their water, their food and their pasture.
sentences.n: ʿudhr, “excuse, plea”. The animals again take the masculine plural -hum, the pronoun for persons. shurūd and shurb, “fleeing” and “drinking”, a play on sound.

sentences.t: فَوَا خَجْلَتِي مِنْ رَبِّي يَوْمَ يُقْتَصُّ لِلشَّاةِ الْجَمَّاءِ مِنَ الشَّاةِ الْقَرْنَاءِ ثُمَّ بَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-wā khajlatī min rabbī yawma yuqtaṣṣu li-al-shāti al-jammāʾi mina al-shāti al-qarnāʾi thumma bakā wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: So O my shame before my Lord, (on the) day (when) retaliation-is-taken for the hornless ewe from the horned ewe! Then he wept and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: How ashamed I shall be before my Lord on the day when the hornless ewe is avenged on the horned!” Then he wept and recited these verses:
sentences.n: wā, the particle of lament: “oh, my shame!” The print sets it apart from khajlatī. The day is the Day of Judgement, when, a well-known ḥadīth says, even the hornless sheep will have justice of the horned one that butted it: no wrong is too small to be weighed. yuqtaṣṣu, “retaliation is exacted”, read here as passive; the active yaqtaṣṣu, “(God) exacts retaliation”, is also possible. The shadda on الجمّاء is the print's own.

sentences.t:
اَمَا وَاللّٰهِ لَوْ عَلِمَ الْاَنَامُ * لِمَا خُلِقُوْا لَمَا غَفَلُوْا وَنَامُوْا
فَمَوْتٌ ثُمَّ بَعْثٌ ثُمَّ حَشْرٌ * وَتَوْبِيخٌ وَاَهْوَالٌ عِظَامُ
وَنَحْنُ اِذَا انْتَهَيْنَا اَوْ اَمَرْنَا * كَاَهْلِ الْكَهْفِ اَيْقَاظٌ نِيَامُ
sentences.tr:
amā wa-allāhi law ʿalima al-anāmu * li-mā khuliqū la-mā ghafalū wa-nāmū
fa-mawtun thumma baʿthun thumma ḥashrun * wa-tawbīkhun wa-ahwālun ʿiẓāmu
wa-naḥnu idhā intahaynā aw amarnā * ka-ahli al-kahfi ayqāẓun niyāmu
sentences.l:
Lo, by God, if mankind knew * for-what they were created, they would not be-heedless and sleep.
For (there is) death, then raising, then gathering, * and rebuke, and terrors mighty.
And we, when we desist or command, * (are) like the people of the cave: awake, asleep.
sentences.i:
By God, if mankind only knew * what they were made for, they would not sleep in heedlessness.
For death is coming, then the raising and the gathering, * the reproach, and terrors past all measure.
Yet we, whether we hold back or give command, * are like the Sleepers of the Cave: awake, and yet asleep.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. amā, “lo, indeed”, opens an oath. baʿth, “raising (of the dead)”, and ḥashr, “gathering (for judgement)”, are the stages of the Last Day; tawbīkh, “reproach”, is the reckoning. The print points انتهينا and امرنا as actives, intahaynā aw amarnā, “we desist or give orders”; the line is usually quoted with passives, nuhīnā aw umirnā, “when we are forbidden or commanded”, which gives the better sense, but the print's vowels are kept. ahl al-kahf, “the people of the cave”, the Seven Sleepers of Qurʾān 18, of whom it is said that one would think them awake though they slept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى عَلَى جُلُوسِهِ تَحْتَ الشَّجَرَةِ عِنْدَ الْعَيْنِ وَمَنْعِهِ الطُّيُورَ وَالْوُحُوشَ مِنْ شُرْبِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma bakā ʿalā julūsihi taḥta al-shajarati ʿinda al-ʿayni wa-manʿihi al-ṭuyūra wa-al-wuḥūsha min shurbihā
sentences.l: Then he wept over his sitting under the tree by the spring and his keeping-back the birds and the wild-beasts from drinking-it.
sentences.i: Then he wept that he had sat beneath the tree by the spring and kept the birds and beasts from drinking there.
sentences.n: julūsihi … wa-manʿihi, two verbal nouns, “his sitting … and his preventing”; manʿ takes its object, al-ṭuyūra, in the accusative like the verb. ʿayn, “eye”, is also “a spring”, as here.

sentences.t: وَوَلَّى سَائِحًا عَلَى وَجْهِهِ حَتَّي أَتَى إِلَى الرَّاعِي فَدَخَلَ إِلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ وَعَانَقَهُ وَبَكَى
sentences.tr: wa-wallā sāʾiḥan ʿalā wajhihi ḥattā atā ilā al-rāʿī fa-dakhala ilayhi wa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhi al-salāma wa-ʿānaqahu wa-bakā
sentences.l: And he turned-away, wandering on his face, until he came to the shepherd; and he entered to him and greeted him, and he returned to him the greeting, and embraced him, and wept.
sentences.i: He turned and wandered off wherever his feet took him, until he came to the shepherd. He went in to him and greeted him, and the shepherd returned his greeting, embraced him and wept.
sentences.n: sāʾiḥ ʿalā wajhihi, “roaming on his face”, going on with no fixed road. حتي is spelled with a dotted yāʾ, as the print often does, for ḥattā. The shepherd is the one who returns the greeting, embraces and weeps; the man of the village, called al-ʿābid, “the worshipper”, is the visitor.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الرَّاعِي مَا الَّذِي أَتَى بِكَ إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي لَمْ يَدْخُلْهُ أَحَدٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-rāʿī mā alladhī atā bika ilā hādhā al-makāni alladhī lam yadkhulhu aḥadun mina al-nāsi ʿalayya
sentences.l: And the shepherd said to him: What (is) it that brought you to this place, which no one of the people has entered upon me?
sentences.i: The shepherd said, “What has brought you to this place, where no one of mankind has ever come in to me?”
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to come with”, that is, “to bring”: mā alladhī atā bika, “what brought you”. dakhala ʿalā, “to come in upon (someone)”, to visit him where he is. The shadda on عليّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْعَابِدُ إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ فِي مَنَامِي مَنْ يَصِفُ لِي مَكَانَكَ وَيَأْمُرُنِي أَنْ أَسِيرَ إِلَيْكَ وَأُسَلِّمَ عَلَيْكَ فَأَتَيْتُكَ مُمْتَثِلًا لِمَا أُمِرْتُ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ʿābidu innī raʾaytu fī manāmī man yaṣifu lī makānaka wa-yaʾmurunī an asīra ilayka wa-usallima ʿalayka fa-ataytuka mumtathilan li-mā umirtu bihi
sentences.l: And the worshipper said to him: Indeed-I saw in my sleep (one) who describes to me your place and commands me that I go to you and greet you; so I came-to you, complying with what I was commanded with.
sentences.i: The hermit said to him, “I saw in a dream someone who described your dwelling to me and bade me go to you and greet you; so I have come to you, obeying what I was commanded.”
sentences.n: The hamza in رأيت is the print's own. amara bi-, “to command (a thing)”: the verb takes its object with bi-, hence li-mā umirtu bihi, “for what I was commanded”. The print marks the passive اُمرتُ with a ḍamma on the alif and on the tāʾ; the marks are kept. imtathala li-, “to comply with, obey”.

sentences.t: فَقَبِلَهُ الرَّاعِي وَطَابَتْ نَفْسُهُ بِصُحْبَتِهِ وَجَلَسَ مَعَهُ فِى الْجَبَلِ يَعْبُدَانِ اللّٰهَ فِي ذَلِكَ الْغَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabilahu al-rāʿī wa-ṭābat nafsuhu bi-ṣuḥbatihi wa-jalasa maʿahu fī al-jabali yaʿbudāni allāha fī dhālika al-ghāri
sentences.l: And the shepherd accepted him, and his soul was-glad with his companionship, and he sat with him in the mountain, the-two worshipping God in that cave.
sentences.i: The shepherd received him and was glad of his company, and he stayed with him on the mountain, the two of them worshipping God in that cave.
sentences.n: قبله can also be read qabbalahu, “he kissed him”; qabilahu, “he accepted him”, suits ṭābat nafsuhu bi-ṣuḥbatihi, “his soul was content with his company”. The verb jalasa is singular, but yaʿbudāni is dual: “the two of them worshipping”. The kasra on the nūn of يعبدانِ is the print's own. ghār, “cave”, the kahf of before.

sentences.t: فَحَسُنَتْ عِبَادَتُهُمَا وَلَمْ يَزَالَا فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ يَعْبُدَانِ رَبَّهُمَا وَيَتَقَوَّتَانِ مِنْ لُحُومِ الْغَنَمِ وَأَلْبَانِهَا مُتَجَرِّدَيْنِ عَنِ الْمَالِ وَالْبَنِينَ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَاهُمَا الْيَقِينُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥasunat ʿibādatuhumā wa-lam yazālā fī dhālika al-makāni yaʿbudāni rabbahumā wa-yataqawwatāni min luḥūmi al-ghanami wa-albānihā mutajarridayni ʿani al-māli wa-al-banīna ilā an atāhumā al-yaqīnu
sentences.l: And their worship became-good, and they-two did not cease in that place worshipping their Lord and taking-sustenance from the meats of the sheep and their milks, stripped-bare of the wealth and the sons, until the certainty came to them.
sentences.i: Their worship grew ever more excellent, and they stayed on in that place worshipping their Lord, living on the flesh and milk of the flock, free of wealth and sons, until the certain end came to them.
sentences.n: yataqawwatāni, “they take as their food (qūt)”. mutajarridayni, dual, “stripped bare of, detached from”: the fatḥa on the dāl is the print's own. al-māl wa-al-banūn, “wealth and sons”, is a Qurʾānic pair for the goods of this world (Qurʾān 18:46). al-yaqīn, “the certainty”, is death, after Qurʾān 15:99, “and worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا آخِرُ حَدِيثِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā ākhiru ḥadīthihimā
sentences.l: And this (is) the end of the tale of-them-two.
sentences.i: And that is the end of their story.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ يَا شَهْرَ زَادُ لَقَدْ زَهَّدْتِنِي فِي مُلْكِي وَنَدَّمْتِنِي عَلَى مَا فَرَطَ مِنِّي فِي قَتْلِ النِّسَاءِ وَالْبَنَاتِ فَهَلْ عِنْدَكِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ حَدِيثِ الطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku yā Shahr Zādu la-qad zahhadtinī fī mulkī wa-naddamtinī ʿalā mā faraṭa minnī fī qatli al-nisāʾi wa-al-banāti fa-hal ʿindaki shayʾun min ḥadīthi al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: And the king said: O Shahrazād, you have indeed made-me-renounce my kingdom, and made-me-repent over what slipped-out from me in the killing of the women and the girls. So is there with you something of the tales of the birds?
sentences.i: Then the king said, “Shahrazād, you have made me weary of my kingdom and sorry for what I did in killing the women and the girls. Have you any more stories of birds?”
sentences.n: The king breaks into the telling, the first sign in some nights that the tales are working on him. zahhada fī, “to make (someone) indifferent to, make him renounce”; naddama ʿalā, “to make (someone) repent of”. faraṭa min, “to slip out from, be done rashly by”. The print spaces the name as two words, شهر زاد. The shadda on منّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam
sentences.l: She said: Yes.
sentences.i: She said: Yes.

sentences.t: زَعَمُوا أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ أَنَّ طَيْرًا مِنَ الطُّيُورِ طَارَ وَعَلَا إِلَى الْجَوِّ ثُمَّ انْقَضَّ عَلَى صَخْرَةٍ فِي وَسَطِ الْمَاءِ وَكَانَ الْمَاءُ جَارِيًا
sentences.tr: zaʿamū ayyuhā al-maliku anna ṭayran mina al-ṭuyūri ṭāra wa-ʿalā ilā al-jawwi thumma inqaḍḍa ʿalā ṣakhratin fī wasaṭi al-māʾi wa-kāna al-māʾu jāriyan
sentences.l: They have claimed, O king, that a bird of the birds flew and rose to the air, then swooped down upon a rock in the middle of the water; and the water was running.
sentences.i: They tell, O king, that a certain bird flew up high into the air and then swooped down onto a rock in the middle of the water, where the water ran swift.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, of the water-bird and the tortoise. zaʿamū, “they claim”, the stock opening of a fable, as in Kalīla wa-Dimna. inqaḍḍa ʿalā, “to swoop down on”, the word for a bird of prey's dive. The shadda on ثمّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا الطَّائِرُ وَاقِفٌ وَإِذَا هُوَ بِرِمَّةِ إِنْسَانٍ جَرَّهَا الْمَاءُ حَتَّى أَسْنَدَهَا إِلَى تِلْكَ الصَّخْرَةِ وَقَدِ انْتَفَخَتْ وَارْتَفَعَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā al-ṭāʾiru wāqifun wa-idhā huwa bi-rimmati insānin jarrahā al-māʾu ḥattā asnadahā ilā tilka al-ṣakhrati wa-qadi intafakhat wa-irtafaʿat
sentences.l: And while the bird (was) standing, behold, he (was) with the corpse of a human, (which) the water dragged until it propped it against that rock; and it had swollen and risen.
sentences.i: While the bird stood there, all at once there was the corpse of a man, carried down by the water until it came to rest against the rock, swollen and floating high.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”, with bi- marking what suddenly appears: wa-idhā huwa bi-rimmati insānin, “and there he was, faced with a man's corpse”. rimma, “decayed remains, a carcass”. The shaddas on رمّة and جرّها are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَدَنَا مِنْهَا طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ وَتَأَمَّلَهَا فَرَآهَا رِمَّةَ ابْنِ آدَمَ فَوَجَدَ فِيهَا ضَرْبَ سُيُوفٍ وَطَعْنَ رِمَاحٍ
sentences.tr: fa-danā minhā ṭayru al-māʾi wa-taʾammalahā fa-raʾāhā rimmata ibni Ādama fa-wajada fīhā ḍarba suyūfin wa-ṭaʿna rimāḥin
sentences.l: And the water-bird drew-near to it and studied it, and saw it (to be) the corpse of a son of Adam; and he found in it the striking of swords and the thrusting of spears.
sentences.i: The water-bird came close and looked it over, and saw that it was the body of a son of Adam, with the marks of sword-blows and spear-thrusts upon it.
sentences.n: Here the bird is named for the first time: ṭayr al-māʾ, “the water-bird”, some kind of waterfowl. ḍarb, “striking”, is the sword's cut; ṭaʿn, “thrusting”, the spear's. The hamzas in تأملها and فرآها, and the madda of آدم, are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَظُنُّ أَنَّ هَذَا الْمَقْتُولَ كَانَ شِرِّيرًا فَاجْتَمَعَ عَلَيْهِ جَمَاعَةٌ فَقَتَلُوهُ وَاسْتَرَاحُوا مِنْهُ وَمِنْ شَرِّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ṭayru al-māʾi fī nafsihi aẓunnu anna hādhā al-maqtūla kāna shirrīran fa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayhi jamāʿatun fa-qatalūhu wa-istarāḥū minhu wa-min sharrihi
sentences.l: And the water-bird said in himself: I think that this slain-one was wicked, so a company gathered against him and killed him and had-rest from him and from his evil.
sentences.i: The water-bird said to himself, “I think this murdered man must have been wicked, so that a band of men joined against him and killed him, and so were rid of him and his evil.”
sentences.n: shirrīr, “very wicked”, an intensive form of sharr, “evil”. ijtamaʿa ʿalā, “to band together against”. istarāḥa min, “to be at rest from, be rid of”. The shaddas on اظنّ and شرّه are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ حَائِرًا وَهُوَ يَتَعَجَّبُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal ṭayru al-māʾi ḥāʾiran wa-huwa yataʿajjabu
sentences.l: And the water-bird did not cease (being) bewildered, and he wondering.
sentences.i: And the water-bird stayed there, at a loss and marvelling.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِنُسُورٍ وَعِقْبَانٍ أَحَاطُوا بِتِلْكَ الْجِيفَةِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ جَوَانِبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-nusūrin wa-ʿiqbānin aḥāṭū bi-tilka al-jīfati min jamīʿi jawānibihā
sentences.l: And while he (was) thus, behold, vultures and eagles surrounded that carrion from all its sides.
sentences.i: While he was so, all at once vultures and eagles came and ringed the carcass round on every side.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what appears. nusūr, “vultures”; ʿiqbān, “eagles”. aḥāṭa bi-, “to surround”. The birds take a masculine plural verb, aḥāṭū, as if they were people; Classical usage would give aḥāṭat. jīfa, “carrion, a rotting carcass”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذَلِكَ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ جَزِعَ جَزَعًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ لَاصَبْرَ لِي عَلَى الْإِقَامَةِ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā dhālika ṭayru al-māʾi jaziʿa jazaʿan shadīdan wa-qāla lā ṣabra lī ʿalā al-iqāmati fī hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: And when the water-bird saw that, he became-alarmed (with) a severe alarm, and said: There-is-no patience for me upon the staying in this place.
sentences.i: When the water-bird saw this he was sorely frightened, and said, “I cannot bear to stay in this place.”
sentences.n: jaziʿa jazaʿan shadīdan, the verb with its own verbal noun, “he was greatly dismayed”. The print runs لا صبر together as لاصبر; the spacing is kept. lā ṣabra lī ʿalā, “I have no endurance for”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَارَ مِنْهُ يُفَتِّشُ عَلَى مَوْضِعٍ يَأْوِيهِ إِلَي حِينِ تَنْفَدُ تِلْكَ الْجِيفَةُ وَتَرُوحُ سِبَاعُ الطُّيُورِ عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma ṭāra minhu yufattishu ʿalā mawḍiʿin yaʾwīhi ilā ḥīni tanfadu tilka al-jīfatu wa-tarūḥu sibāʿu al-ṭuyūri ʿanhā
sentences.l: Then he flew from it, searching for a spot (that) would shelter him until the time (that) that carrion is-used-up and the beasts-of-prey of the birds go from it.
sentences.i: Then he flew off, looking for somewhere to shelter until the carcass was finished and the birds of prey had gone from it.
sentences.n: fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, a colloquial construction; Classical Arabic says fattasha ʿan. The hamza in يأويه is the print's own; yaʾwīhi, “(a place) that would shelter him”. الي is spelled with a dotted yāʾ for ilā. sibāʿ al-ṭuyūr, “the beasts of prey among the birds”, the raptors.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ طَائِرًا حَتَّى وَجَدَ نَهْرًا فِي وَسَطِهِ شَجَرَةٌ فَنَزَلَ عَلَيْهَا مُتَغَيِّرًا كَئِيبًا حَزِينًا عَلَى فِرَاقِ وَطَنِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal ṭāʾiran ḥattā wajada nahran fī wasaṭihi shajaratun fa-nazala ʿalayhā mutaghayyiran kaʾīban ḥazīnan ʿalā firāqi waṭanihi
sentences.l: And he did not cease flying until he found a river, in its middle a tree; and he alighted on it, changed, dejected, sad over the parting from his homeland.
sentences.i: He flew on and on until he found a river with a tree in the middle of it, and he settled on it, troubled, dejected and grieving at being parted from his home.
sentences.n: mutaghayyir, “changed”, here “troubled, out of sorts”. waṭan, “homeland, home”, the place one belongs to.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَا زَالَتِ الْأَحْزَانُ تَتْبَعُنِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi mā zālati al-aḥzānu tatbaʿunī
sentences.l: And he said in himself: The sorrows have not ceased following me.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “Sorrows never stop following me.

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ قَدِ اسْتَرَحْتُ لَمَّا رَأَيْتُ تِلْكَ الْجِيفَةَ وَفَرِحْتُ بِهَا فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَقُلْتُ هَذَا رِزْقٌ سَاقَهُ اللّٰهُ إِلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu qadi istaraḥtu lammā raʾaytu tilka al-jīfata wa-fariḥtu bihā faraḥan shadīdan wa-qultu hādhā rizqun sāqahu allāhu ilayya
sentences.l: And I had been-at-ease when I saw that carrion, and I rejoiced in it a great joy, and I said: This (is) a provision (that) God has driven to me.
sentences.i: I was easy in my mind when I saw that carcass, and rejoiced over it greatly, and said, ‘This is a provision God has sent my way.’
sentences.n: The water-bird had first seen the carcass as food, rizq, “provision, daily bread”, which God “drives” (sāqa) to His creatures. The hamza in رأيت and the shadda on اليّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ فَرَحِي غَمًّا وَسُرُورِي حُزْنًا وَهَمًّا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra faraḥī ghamman wa-surūrī ḥuznan wa-hamman
sentences.l: And my joy became grief, and my gladness sorrow and care.
sentences.i: But my joy has turned to grief, and my gladness to sorrow and care.
sentences.n: The print has وسرري, a misprint for وسروري, corrected here. ghamm and hamm, “grief” and “anxiety”, chime with each other, a little rhyme in the bird's complaint. The shadda on همّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهَا وَافْتَرَسَتْهَا سِبَاعُ الطُّيُورِ مِنِّي وَحَالُوا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathā wa-iftarasathā sibāʿu al-ṭuyūri minnī wa-ḥālū baynī wa-baynahā
sentences.l: For the beasts-of-prey of the birds took it and tore-it-as-prey from me, and they came-between me and it.
sentences.i: The birds of prey seized it from me and tore it apart, and came between me and it.
sentences.n: The verbs first agree with sibāʿ, a broken plural, in the feminine singular, akhadhat … iftarasat (the sukūns on their tāʾ are the print's own), then switch to the masculine plural, ḥālū, as if the birds were men. ḥāla bayna … wa-bayna, “to come between, keep apart”.

sentences.t: فَكَيْفَ أَرْجُوأَنْ أَكُونَ سَالِمًا فِى هَذِةِ الدُّنْيَا مِنَ الْكَدَرِ وَأَطْمَئِنَّ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-kayfa arjū an akūna sāliman fī hādhihi al-dunyā mina al-kadari wa-aṭmaʾinna ilayhā
sentences.l: So how (can) I hope that I be safe in this world from the turbidity, and that I trust-at-ease in it?
sentences.i: How then can I hope to be safe from trouble in this world, or to rest secure in it?
sentences.n: The print runs ارجو ان together as ارجوان; the spacing is kept. هذة is spelled with tāʾ marbūṭa for هذه, hādhihi. kadar, “muddiness”, of water, and so “trouble, what spoils life”. iṭmaʾanna ilā, “to feel secure in, rely on”; the hamza seat in اطمئن is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ قِيلَ فِى الْمَثَلِ الدُّنْيَا دَارُ مَنْ لَا دَارَ لَهُ يَغْتَرُّبِهَا مَنْ لَا عَقْلَ لَهُ وَيَطْمَئِنُّ إِلَيْهَا بِمَالِهِ وَوَلَدِهِ وَقَوْمِهِ وَعَشِيرَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad qīla fī al-mathali al-dunyā dāru man lā dāra lahu yaghtarru bihā man lā ʿaqla lahu wa-yaṭmaʾinnu ilayhā bi-mālihi wa-waladihi wa-qawmihi wa-ʿashīratihi
sentences.l: And it has been said in the proverb: The world (is) the house of (him) who has no house; is-deceived by it (he) who has no reason, and trusts-at-ease in it with his wealth and his children and his people and his clan.
sentences.i: As the proverb says: This world is the home of him who has no home; it deceives the man who has no sense, who rests secure in it with his wealth and children, his people and his kin.
sentences.n: The first clause is a saying of the ascetics: the true home is the next world, and only one who has none there makes this world his house. The print runs يغترّ بها together as يغترّبها; the spacing is kept. ightarra bi-, “to be deluded by, put false trust in”. The shaddas on يغترّبها and يطمئنّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلِ الْمُغْتَرُّبِهَا رَاكِنًا إِلَيْهَا يَخْتَالُ فَوْقَ الْأَرْضِ حَتَّى يَصِيرَ تَحْتَهَا وَيَحْثُوَ عَلَيْهِ التُّرَابَ أَعَزُّ النَّاسِ إِلَيْهِ وَأَقْرَبُهُمْ الَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazali al-mughtarru bihā rākinan ilayhā yakhtālu fawqa al-arḍi ḥattā yaṣīra taḥtahā wa-yaḥthuwa ʿalayhi al-turāba aʿazzu al-nāsi ilayhi wa-aqrabuhum ladayhi
sentences.l: And the deluded-by-it does not cease leaning on it, strutting above the earth, until he comes-to-be beneath it, and the dearest of people to him and the nearest of them with him scatter upon him the dust.
sentences.i: And the man deluded by it goes on relying on it, strutting proudly over the earth, until he lies beneath it, and those dearest and closest to him throw the dust down upon him.
sentences.n: The print runs المغترّ بها together as المغترّبها; the spacing is kept, and the shadda is the print's own. rakana ilā, “to lean on, trust in”; ikhtāla, “to strut, walk proudly”. fawqa al-arḍi … taḥtahā, “above the earth … beneath it”, a stock antithesis. ḥathā, “to scatter (dust)”, as mourners do at a grave. The print has الديه, which makes no word; it is read here as ladayhi, “with him, near him”, with a stray alif, though اليه, ilayhi, repeated from the clause before, is also possible.

sentences.t: وَمَا لِلْفَتَى خَيْرٌ مِنَ الصَّبْرِ عَلَى هُمُومِهَا وَمَكَارِهِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-mā li-al-fatā khayrun mina al-ṣabri ʿalā humūmihā wa-makārihihā
sentences.l: And there-is-not for the young-man (anything) better than the patience over its cares and its hateful-things.
sentences.i: Nothing serves a man better than to bear its cares and hardships with patience.
sentences.n: fatā, “young man”, in wisdom sayings simply “a man”. makārih, “things one hates, hardships”, from kariha, “to dislike”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ فَارَقْتُ مَكَانِي وَوَطَنِي وَكُنْتُ كَارِهًا لِفُرْقَةِ إِخْوَانِي وَأَحِبَّائِي وَخِلَّانِي
sentences.tr: wa-qad fāraqtu makānī wa-waṭanī wa-kuntu kārihan li-furqati ikhwānī wa-aḥibbāʾī wa-khillānī
sentences.l: And I have parted-from my place and my homeland, and I was hating the separation from my brothers and my loved-ones and my close-friends.
sentences.i: And now I have left my place and my home, though I was loath to be parted from my brothers, my loved ones and my friends.”
sentences.n: ikhwān, aḥibbāʾ, khillān, “brothers, loved ones, intimate friends”, rhyme on -ān/-āʾ, the closing cadence of the bird's lament. The tanwīn on كارهًا, the hamza seat in احبائي and the shadda on خلّاني are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ فِي فِكْرَتِهِ وَإِذَا بِذَكَرٍ مِنَ السَّلَاحِفِ أَقْبَلَ مُنْحَدِرًا فِى الْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa fī fikratihi wa-idhā bi-dhakarin mina al-salāḥifi aqbala munḥadiran fī al-māʾi
sentences.l: And while he (was) in his thought, behold, a male of the tortoises came, going-down in the water.
sentences.i: While he was lost in thought, all at once a male tortoise came swimming down the stream.
sentences.n: salāḥif, “tortoises”, plural of sulaḥfāh. dhakar, “a male”: the tortoise is a he. munḥadiran, “going downstream”. The fatḥa on the dhāl of بذَكر is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَدَنَا مِنْ طَيْرِ الْمَاءِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ يَا سَيِّدِي مَا الَّذِي حَجَبَكَ وَأَبْعَدَكَ عَنْ مَوْضِعِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-danā min ṭayri al-māʾi wa-sallama ʿalayhi wa-qāla yā sayyidī mā alladhī ḥajabaka wa-abʿadaka ʿan mawḍiʿika
sentences.l: And he drew-near to the water-bird and greeted him and said: O my lord, what (is) it that has screened you and taken-you-far from your spot?
sentences.i: He came close to the water-bird, greeted him, and said, “Sir, what has shut you out and driven you so far from your home?”
sentences.n: ḥajaba, “to veil, screen off”, here “to keep (someone) away”. The shadda on سلّم is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَ حُلُولُ الْأَعْدَاءِ فِيهِ وَلَا صَبْرَ لِلْعَاقِلِ عَلَى مُجَاوَرَةِ عَدُوِّهِ وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ بَعْضِ الشُّعَرَاءِ
sentences.tr: qāla ḥulūlu al-aʿdāʾi fīhi wa-lā ṣabra li-al-ʿāqili ʿalā mujāwarati ʿaduwwihi wa-mā aḥsana qawla baʿḍi al-shuʿarāʾi
sentences.l: He said: The alighting of the enemies in it; and there-is-no patience for the sensible-one upon the neighbouring of his enemy. And how beautiful (is) the saying of one of the poets:
sentences.i: He said, “Enemies have settled there, and no man of sense can bear to live next door to his foe. How well a poet has put it:
sentences.n: ḥulūl, “alighting, settling in a place”. mujāwara, “living as a neighbour”. mā aḥsana, the exclamatory form, “how fine is …!”. The shadda on عدوّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: اِذَا حَلَّ الثَّقِيْلُ بِاَرْضِ قَوْمٍ * فَمَا لِلسَّاكِنِيْنِ سِوَى الرَّحِيْلِ
sentences.tr: idhā ḥalla al-thaqīlu bi-arḍi qawmin * fa-mā li-al-sākinīna siwā al-raḥīli
sentences.l: When the burdensome-one alights in the land of a people, * then there-is-not for the dwellers (anything) but the departure.
sentences.i: When a tiresome guest settles in a people's land, * nothing is left for those who live there but to leave.”
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. thaqīl, “heavy”, of a person “tiresome, a bore, unwelcome”, a stock figure in Arabic verse and anecdote. raḥīl, “departure, setting off”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ السِّحْلِفُ إِنْ كَانَ الْأَمْرُ كَمَا وَصَفْتَهُ وَالْحَالُ مِثْلُ ذَكَرْتَهُ فَأَنَا لَاأَزَالُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ وَلَا أُفَارِقُكَ لِأَقْضِيَ لَكَ حَاجَتَكَ وَاِنِّي بِخِدْمَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-siḥlifu in kāna al-amru kamā waṣaftahu wa-al-ḥālu mithlu dhakartahu fa-anā lā azālu bayna yadayka wa-lā ufāriquka li-aqḍiya laka ḥājataka wa-innī bi-khidmatika
sentences.l: And the tortoise said to him: If the matter is as you-described-it, and the state like you-mentioned-it, then I — I-shall-not-cease (to be) between your two hands, and I-shall-not part-from-you, so-as-to fulfil for you your need; and indeed-I (am) at your service.
sentences.i: The tortoise answered, “If things are as you describe and your plight is as you tell it, then I will stay by your side and never leave you, and see to whatever you need: I am at your service.
sentences.n: al-siḥlif is the print's spelling, here and throughout, of the tortoise (sulaḥfāʾ / sulaḥfāh). mithlu dhakartahu, “like you mentioned it”: the mā that Classical Arabic wants after mithl (mithla mā) is left out. bayna yadayka, “between your two hands”, in your presence, at your disposal. The print runs lā azālu together as لاازال; the spacing is kept. The kasra in واِني is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ قِيلَ لَا وَحْشَةَ أَشَدُّ مِنْ وَحْشَةِ الْغَرِيبِ الْمُنْقَطِعِ عَنْ أَهْلِهِ وَوَطَنِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu qīla lā waḥshata ashaddu min waḥshati al-gharībi al-munqaṭiʿi ʿan ahlihi wa-waṭanihi
sentences.l: For it has been said: (There is) no loneliness harsher than the loneliness of the stranger cut-off from his people and his homeland.
sentences.i: For it is said that no loneliness is harsher than that of the stranger cut off from his people and his home.
sentences.n: waḥsha, “desolation, the loneliness of being among strangers”. gharīb, “stranger”, one far from home. The shadda on اشدّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ قِيلَ إِنَّ فُرْقَةَ الصَّالِحِينَ لَا يُعَدُّ لَهَا شَيْءٌ مِنَ الْمَصَائِبِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad qīla inna furqata al-ṣāliḥīna lā yuʿaddu lahā shayʾun mina al-maṣāʾibi
sentences.l: And it has been said that the parting-from the righteous, there-is-not reckoned to-it a thing of the calamities.
sentences.i: It is also said that no calamity is equal to parting from good friends.
sentences.n: lā yuʿaddu lahā shayʾun, “nothing is reckoned against it”, i.e. nothing matches it. The two words could also be one, يعدلها, yaʿdiluhā, “equals it”, which comes to the same; the print sets two words and they are read as printed. furqa, “separation, parting”. al-ṣāliḥūn, “the righteous, good people”, here the good companions one leaves.

sentences.t: وَأَحْسَنُ مَا يُسَلِّي بِهِ الْعَاقِلُ نَفْسَهُ الِاسْتِينَاسُ فِى الْغُرْبَةِ وَالصَّبْرُ عَلَى الرَّزِيَّةِ وَالْكُرْبَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-aḥsanu mā yusallī bihi al-ʿāqilu nafsahu al-istīnāsu fī al-ghurbati wa-al-ṣabru ʿalā al-raziyyati wa-al-kurbati
sentences.l: And the best (of) what the wise-man consoles with-it himself (is) the finding-of-company in the exile, and the patience over the misfortune and the distress.
sentences.i: The best consolation a wise man can find is to make friends in a strange land and to bear misfortune and distress with patience.
sentences.n: sallā nafsahu bi-, “to console oneself with”. al-istīnās, “taking comfort in company, growing at ease”, Classical istiʾnās with the hamza softened to ī. ghurba, “being away from home, exile”. raziyya, “calamity”, for razīʾa. ghurba and kurba rhyme. The shadda in يسلّي and the vowels on العاقلُ and نفسَه are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَرْجُو أَنْ تَحْمَدَ صُحْبَتِي مَعَكَ وَأَكُونَ لَكَ خَادِمًا وَمُعِينًا
sentences.tr: wa-arjū an taḥmada ṣuḥbatī maʿaka wa-akūna laka khādiman wa-muʿīnan
sentences.l: And I hope that you-will-praise my companionship with you, and (that) I-shall-be for you a servant and a helper.
sentences.i: I hope you will find me a good companion, and that I may be your servant and your helper.”
sentences.n: ḥamida, “to praise, find good”: “that you will have cause to praise my company”. khādim and muʿīn, “servant” and “helper”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ مَقَالَةَ السِّحْلِفِ قَالَ لَهُ لَقَدْ صَدَقْتَ فِي قَوْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ṭayru al-māʾi maqālata al-siḥlifi qāla lahu la-qad ṣadaqta fī qawlika
sentences.l: And when the water-bird heard the speech of the tortoise, he said to him: You have indeed spoken-true in your saying.
sentences.i: When the water-bird heard the tortoise's words, he said, “You speak the truth.
sentences.n: maqāla, “saying, words spoken”. la-qad with the past, an emphatic “indeed”.

sentences.t: وَلَعَمْرِي إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ لِلْفِرَاقِ أَلَمًا وَغَمًّا مُدَّةَ بُعْدِي عَنْ مَكَانِي وَفِرَاقِي لِإِخْوَانِي وَخِلَّانِي
sentences.tr: wa-la-ʿamrī innī wajadtu li-al-firāqi alaman wa-ghamman muddata buʿdī ʿan makānī wa-firāqī li-ikhwānī wa-khillānī
sentences.l: And by-my-life, indeed-I found for the parting a pain and a grief, (during the) span of my distance from my place and my parting from my brothers and my close-friends.
sentences.i: Upon my life, I have known the pain and sorrow of parting all the while I have been far from my home and separated from my brothers and my friends.
sentences.n: la-ʿamrī, “by my life”, a common oath. wajada, “to find”, also “to feel”: wajada alaman, “he felt pain”. khillān (sing. khalīl), “close friends”. The shadda in خلّاني and the vowels on مدةَ and بُعدي are the print's own.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّ فِى الْفِرَاقِ عِبْرَةً لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ وَفِكْرَةً لِمَنْ تَفَكَّرَ
sentences.tr: li-anna fī al-firāqi ʿibratan li-mani iʿtabara wa-fikratan li-man tafakkara
sentences.l: Because in the parting (is) a lesson for whoever takes-a-lesson, and a reflection for whoever reflects.
sentences.i: For in parting there is a lesson for anyone who will learn, and matter for thought for anyone who will think.
sentences.n: ʿibra … liman iʿtabara, fikra … liman tafakkara: noun and verb from the same root each time, and the two verbs rhyme. The shadda in تفكّر is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا لَمْ يَجِدِ الْفَتَى مَنْ يُسَلِّيهِ مِنَ الْأَصْحَابِ يَنْقَطِعُ عَنْهُ الْخَيْرُ أَبَدًا وَيَثْبُتُ الشَّرُّ سَرْمَدًا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā lam yajidi al-fatā man yusallīhi mina al-aṣḥābi yanqaṭiʿu ʿanhu al-khayru abadan wa-yathbutu al-sharru sarmadan
sentences.l: And when the young-man does-not find (someone) who consoles-him of the companions, the good is-cut-off from him for-ever, and the evil stays-fixed everlastingly.
sentences.i: When a man finds no friend to comfort him, good is cut off from him for ever, and evil stays with him for good.
sentences.n: fatā, “young man”, often simply “a man, anyone”. After idhā the answer is a plain present, yanqaṭiʿu, where Classical Arabic would use a past tense or fa-. abadan and sarmadan, “for ever” and “everlastingly”, rhyme. The shadda in يسلّيه is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ لِلْعَاقِلِ إِلَّا التَّسَلِّي بِالْإِخْوَانِ عَنِ الْهُمُومِ فِي جَمِيعِ الْأَحْوَالِ وَمُلَازَمَةُ الصَّبْرِ وَالتَّجَلُّدِ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa li-al-ʿāqili illā al-tasallī bi-al-ikhwāni ʿani al-humūmi fī jamīʿi al-aḥwāli wa-mulāzamatu al-ṣabri wa-al-tajalludi
sentences.l: And there-is-not for the wise-man except the consoling-oneself with the brothers from the cares in all the circumstances, and the clinging-to the patience and the fortitude.
sentences.i: A wise man has nothing for it but to seek comfort for his cares in his friends, whatever befalls, and to hold fast to patience and endurance;
sentences.n: tasallā bi- … ʿan, “to find comfort in (something) from (a sorrow)”. mulāzama, “keeping to, clinging to”. tajallud, “steeling oneself, fortitude”. The shadda in الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُمَا خَصْلَتَانِ مَحْمُودَتَانِ يُعِينَانِ عَلَي الْمُصِيبَةِ وَنَوَائِبِ الدَّهْرِ وَيَدْفَعَانِ الْفَزَعَ وَالْجَزَعَ فِي كُلِّ أَمْرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-innahumā khaṣlatāni maḥmūdatāni yuʿīnāni ʿalā al-muṣībati wa-nawāʾibi al-dahri wa-yadfaʿāni al-fazaʿa wa-al-jazaʿa fī kulli amrin
sentences.l: For they-two (are) two praiseworthy qualities; they-help against the calamity and the blows of the time, and they-ward-off the fright and the anguish in every matter.
sentences.i: for these two are praiseworthy qualities: they help a man against misfortune and the blows of fate, and keep fear and despair from him in everything.”
sentences.n: The print spells ʿalā here with ي, علي; it is pointed as the preposition. aʿāna ʿalā, “to help against”. nawāʾib al-dahr, “the blows of time”, the strokes of fortune. fazaʿ and jazaʿ, “fright” and “anguish, loss of composure”, rhyme.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ السِّحْلِفُ إِيَّاكَ وَالْجَزَعَ فَإِنَّهُ يُفْسِدُ عَلَيْكَ عَيْشَكَ وَيُذْهِبُ مُرُوَّتَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-siḥlifu iyyāka wa-al-jazaʿa fa-innahu yufsidu ʿalayka ʿayshaka wa-yudhhibu muruwwataka
sentences.l: And the tortoise said to him: Beware-you and the anguish! For it spoils for you your living and takes-away your manliness.
sentences.i: The tortoise said, “Beware of despair, for it will spoil your life and rob you of your dignity.”
sentences.n: iyyāka wa-…, “beware of …”, the warning construction: “keep yourself and (keep away) the …”. muruwwa, Classical murūʾa, “manliness, the bearing of a self-respecting man”: the hamza has become a doubled wāw, as in speech. The shadda on the wāw is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالَا يَتَحَدَّثَانِ مَعَ بَعْضِهِمَا إِلَى أَنْ قَالَ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ لِلسِّحْلِفِ أَنَا لَمْ أَزَلْ أَخْشَى نَوَائِبَ الزَّمَانِ وَطَوَارِقَ الْحَدَثَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zālā yataḥaddathāni maʿa baʿḍihimā ilā an qāla ṭayru al-māʾi li-al-siḥlifi anā lam azal akhshā nawāʾiba al-zamāni wa-ṭawāriqa al-ḥadathāni
sentences.l: And they-two did-not cease talking with each-other until the water-bird said to the tortoise: I — I-have-not ceased fearing the blows of the time and the night-comers of the mishaps.
sentences.i: The two went on talking together, until the water-bird said to the tortoise, “I have never stopped fearing the blows of fortune and the sudden strokes of fate.”
sentences.n: maʿa baʿḍihimā, “with each other”, an everyday turn for the Classical baʿḍuhumā maʿa baʿḍin. ṭawāriq (sing. ṭāriqa), “things that come by night”, sudden calamities; ḥadathān, “the vicissitudes of fortune”. zamān and ḥadathān rhyme. The shadda in يتحدّثان is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السِّحْلِفُ مَقَالَةَ طَيْرِ الْمَاءِ أَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَهُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-siḥlifu maqālata ṭayri al-māʾi aqbala ʿalayhi wa-qabbalahu bayna ʿaynayhi
sentences.l: And when the tortoise heard the speech of the water-bird, he came-up to him and kissed-him between his two eyes,
sentences.i: When the tortoise heard the water-bird's words, he went up to him and kissed him between the eyes,
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to come towards, turn to”; qabbala, “to kiss”: the two verbs share a root, q-b-l. Kissing between the eyes is a gesture of affection and comfort. The shadda in قبّله is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ لَمْ تَزَلْ جَمَاعَةُ الطَّيْرِ تَتَبَرَّكُ بِكَ وَتَعْرِفُ فِي مَشُورَتِكَ الْخَيْرَ فَكَيْفَ تَحْمِلُ الْهَمَّ وَالضَّيْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu lam tazal jamāʿatu al-ṭayri tatabarraku bika wa-taʿrifu fī mashūratika al-khayra fa-kayfa taḥmilu al-hamma wa-al-ḍayra
sentences.l: And he said to him: The company of the birds has-not ceased seeking-blessing from you and knowing in your counsel the good; so how do-you-carry the care and the harm?
sentences.i: and said to him, “The birds have always looked on you as a blessing and found good in your counsel; so why do you burden yourself with worry and fear of harm?”
sentences.n: tabarraka bi-, “to seek a blessing from, count lucky”. mashūra, “counsel, advice”. ḍayr, “harm”. khayr and ḍayr rhyme, and so does hamm. The shadda in الهمّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يُسَكِّنُ رَوْعَ طَيْرِ الْمَاءِ حَتَّى اطْمَأَنَّ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal yusakkinu rawʿa ṭayri al-māʾi ḥattā iṭmaʾanna
sentences.l: And he did-not cease calming the fright of the water-bird until he was-at-ease.
sentences.i: And he went on calming the water-bird's fears until he was at peace.
sentences.n: rawʿ, “fright, alarm”. iṭmaʾanna, “to be reassured, set at rest”. The hamza and shadda of اطمأنّ are the print's own, as is the shadda in يسكّن.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ طَيْرَ الْمَاءِ طَارَ إِلَى مَكَانِ الْجِيفَةِ فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ لَمْ يَرَ مِنْ سِبَاعِ الطَّيْرِ شَيْأً وَلَا مِنْ تِلْكَ الْجِيفَةِ إِلَّاعِظَامًا
sentences.tr: thumma inna ṭayra al-māʾi ṭāra ilā makāni al-jīfati fa-lammā waṣala ilayhi lam yara min sibāʿi al-ṭayri shayʾan wa-lā min tilka al-jīfati illā ʿiẓāman
sentences.l: Then the water-bird flew to the place of the carrion; and when he reached it, he did-not see of the beasts-of-prey of the birds a thing, nor of that carrion except bones.
sentences.i: Then the water-bird flew to the place where the carcass had lain; and when he got there he saw not one of the birds of prey, and nothing of the carcass but bones.
sentences.n: jīfa, “carrion, a rotting carcass”: the one the birds of prey had gathered round. sibāʿ al-ṭayr, “the predators among birds”; sabuʿ is any beast of prey. lam yara, jussive of raʾā, “he did not see”. shayʾan is spelt شيأ, as the print usually spells it. The print runs illā ʿiẓāman together as الّاعظاما; the spacing is kept, and the shadda is its own.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَ وَأَخْبَرَ السِّحْلِفَ بِزَوَالِ الْعَدُوِّ مِنْ مَكَانِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿa wa-akhbara al-siḥlifa bi-zawāli al-ʿaduwwi min makānihi
sentences.l: And he returned and informed the tortoise of the departure of the enemy from his place.
sentences.i: He went back and told the tortoise that the enemy had left the place.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: the verb takes bi-. zawāl, “ceasing, passing away, removal”. The shadda in العدوّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي أُحِبُّ الرُّجُوعَ إِلَى مَكَانِي لِأَتَمَلَّى بِخِلَّانِي فَإِنَّهُ لَا صَبْرَ لِلْعَاقِلِ عَلَى فِرَاقِ وَطَنِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu iʿlam annī uḥibbu al-rujūʿa ilā makānī li-atamallā bi-khillānī fa-innahu lā ṣabra li-al-ʿāqili ʿalā firāqi waṭanihi
sentences.l: And he said to him: Know that I love the returning to my place, so-as-to enjoy-to-the-full my close-friends; for there-is no patience for the wise-man over the parting-from his homeland.
sentences.i: And he said, “I should like to go back to my own place and enjoy the company of my friends; for no sensible creature can bear to be parted from his home.”
sentences.n: tamallā bi-, “to enjoy (something) to the full”. The print runs li-atamallā together as لاتملّى; the spacing is kept. The shaddas in انّي, احبّ, لاتملّى and بخلّاني are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَتَيَا إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ فَلَمْ يَجِدَا شَيْأً مِمَّا يَخَافَا مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-atayā ilā dhālika al-makāni fa-lam yajidā shayʾan mimmā yakhāfā minhu
sentences.l: And the two came to that place, and they-did-not find a thing of-what they-were-afraid of-it.
sentences.i: So the two of them went to that place, and found nothing there of what they had feared.
sentences.n: yakhāfā, “they (two) fear”, is the dual without its final -ni (Classical yakhāfāni), a Middle Arabic form found elsewhere in this text.

sentences.t: فَأَنْشَدَ طَيْرُ الْمَاءِ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-anshada ṭayru al-māʾi yaqūlu
sentences.l: And the water-bird recited, saying:
sentences.i: And the water-bird recited:

sentences.t:
وَلَرُبَّ نَازِلَةٍ يَضِيقُ لَهَا الْفَتَى * ذَرْعًا وَعِنْدَ اللّٰهِ مِنْهَا الْمَخْرَجُ
ضَاقَتْ فَلَمَّا اسْتَمْكَنَتْ حَلَقَاتُهَا * فَرَجَتْ وَكُنْتُ اَظُنُّهَا لَاتُفْرَجُ
sentences.tr:
wa-la-rubba nāzilatin yaḍīqu lahā al-fatā * dharʿan wa-ʿinda allāhi minhā al-makhraju
ḍāqat fa-lammā istamkanat ḥalaqātuhā * farajat wa-kuntu aẓunnuhā lā tufraju
sentences.l:
And many-a calamity the young-man is-straitened by-it in-capacity, * and with God (is) from-it the way-out.
It grew-tight, and when its rings were-firmly-fixed, * it opened, and I used-to think-it would-not be-opened.
sentences.i:
Many a blow of fortune leaves a man at the end of his strength, * and yet with God lies the way out of it.
